title: Break Your Own Link: What One Fault Costs

questions.question: A link loses one byte in a hundred from the middle of its frames. Before measuring, how many messages is each lost byte likely to cost?
options: None, since the checksum repairs it
Nearly two, because the parser takes the bytes it was promised from the start of the next frame
It depends on the baud rate
One, the message the byte belonged to
questions.explanation: The parser was told a length and waits for that many bytes. When one is missing it takes the shortfall from the next frame, so two frames are damaged by one lost byte.

questions.question: Why is a flipped bit cheaper than a dropped byte?
options: A flipped bit is always corrected by the checksum
The parser ignores them
Flipped bits are rarer
The frame keeps its length, so the checksum rejects exactly that frame and the stream stays in step
questions.explanation: Measured, a flip cost 1.01 to 1.07 frames and a drop cost 1.72 to 1.89. The difference is whether the length the parser was promised is still true.

questions.question: Why are the fault rates given in parts per million as integers rather than as a fraction?
options: The standard fixes the random engines but not the distributions, so a floating point decision can differ between compilers; an integer comparison cannot
Integers are faster
It is the convention for serial ports
Fractions cannot be less than one
questions.explanation: A test asserts a number measured on one machine. That only holds on the others if the same seed gives the same faults everywhere, which needs an owned generator and an integer comparison.

questions.question: At one dropped byte in a hundred, 873 misaligned frames failed the checksum and 3 passed it with the wrong content. What predicts the 3?
options: Three bytes were flipped
A bug in the checksum
The parser dropped them deliberately
A misaligned frame is arbitrary data to an eight bit check, which it matches one time in 256, and 876 divided by 256 is 3.4
questions.explanation: Luck, and a calculable amount of it. A wider check makes it rarer by a factor you can compute, which is the next lesson.

questions.question: A test injects only bit flips and finds the eight bit CRC never lets a wrong frame through. What is wrong with the conclusion?
options: CRC-8 detects every single bit error by construction, so the test could never find the failure; dropped bytes make misaligned frames that pass about one in 256
Flips are too rare to count
The test should flip two bits
Nothing, the CRC is perfect
questions.explanation: The fault the test chose is the one the check is guaranteed to catch. The fault that gets through is a different kind of damage, and only a test that injects it can see it.

questions.question: A seed of zero is given to a xorshift generator and a test injecting faults passes with none injected. Why?
options: Zero means random
The port ignored the seed
The state of a xorshift generator stays at zero for ever, so it never produces a fault
Zero is an invalid rate
questions.explanation: Xor and shift of zero is zero. A seed of zero must become something else, or the test passes for the wrong reason.
